summary.text: A female infant born at 37^(+6) weeks by spontaneous vaginal delivery through grade III meconium-stained fluid, with birth weight 2,700 g and non-consanguineous parents, developed a generalized urticarial-like rash on the first day of life and was admitted to a local NICU for concern of early-onset sepsis with elevated WBC and CRP. Broad-spectrum antibiotics and intravenous methylprednisolone did not control the rash.

Transferred to the tertiary NICU on the 8th day of life, she had frontal bossing, a widespread urticarial rash, palpable axillary lymphadenopathy, knee and ankle arthropathy and recurrent fever. CSF on day 9 showed pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose; cranial MRI on day 14 was unremarkable; AABR showed a refer result in the left ear; microbiology was negative. Antibiotics, fluconazole, IVIG and methylprednisolone gave only transient and incomplete control.

Whole-exome sequencing found a heterozygous NLRP3 c.2263G>A (p.Gly755Arg) variant, absent in both parents (de novo) and interpreted as pathogenic, confirming NOMID after infection, TORCH and neonatal lupus were considered and HLH criteria were absent.

Subcutaneous canakinumab started at 48 days of life led to resolution of rash and fever within 24 h and normalized inflammatory markers; after a transient CRP rise to 10 mg/L the dose was increased to 3 mg/kg every 8 weeks, with clinical and serological remission over 13 months of follow-up, normalized hearing and developmental milestones, no recurrence or treatment-related complications reported, and conflicting statements about growth.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 4
Longitudinal changes in white blood cell count and C-reactive protein following canakinumab treatment in a case of neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease. The red arrow indicates the time of definitive diagnosis and initiation of canakinumab treatment. The black annotation denotes the canakinumab dosage of 2 mg/(kg·day). During follow-up, a mild elevation in both white blood cell (WBC) count and C-reactive protein (CRP) was observed. After the dosage was adjusted to 3 mg/kg/day, both WBC and CRP decreased to within the normal range.

article_limitations: The 52-case systematic review (Supplementary Tables S1 and S4, Figure 1) and its cohort percentages are aggregate/literature data; the other cases are not roster patients.
Supplementary Table S2 lists CSF cells as 23 on D9 and 105 on D12, whereas the text gives 105 on day 9.
Figure 4 shows a red arrow at d43 for diagnosis and canakinumab initiation, while the text and Supplementary Table S2 give 48 days of life.
Figure 1 PRISMA identifies 160 records and 147 PubMed plus 14 Chinese database records; the text states 161 records.
Canakinumab dose units in the Figure 4 caption (per day) differ from the text (every 8 weeks); kept as printed and not reconciled.
Growth after canakinumab and the statement that all monitored parameters remained normal conflict with other statements in the article; both sides are retained as review-only.

Supplementary Table S2 places the CRP peak (67.40 mg/L) at D16-17, while Figure 4 plots the CRP peak at the d15 label; not reconciled.
